items: Pushing from an old local branch whose upstream is gone. Root cause: pruning removes the remote-tracking ref but keeps the local branch and its upstream setting, so a push creates the branch on the server again.
Believing git branch -r lists the server's branches. Root cause: it lists remote-tracking refs in your clone, which a default fetch never deletes.
Pushing a topic branch to the shared repository in a fork setup. Root cause: without remote.pushDefault or branch.<name>.pushRemote, a branch created from upstream/main has upstream as its remote.
Setting fetch.prune=true everywhere and counting on clones as a safety net. Root cause: pruning deletes the ref and its reflog, which may be the last name of commits that were deleted by mistake.
Giving one remote a fetch URL and a push URL that are different repositories. Root cause: the manual requires both to lead to the same repository; two places need two remotes.

slides.body: Today you kept two remotes apart, and you made a zombie branch on purpose, so you'll recognise one when it turns up.

beats.text: A branch that the team merged and deleted a month ago is back on the server. Nobody intended it. It carries old commits, it shows up in the branch list, and by Thursday somebody has built a new feature on top of it.
beats.tele: A branch that the team merged and deleted a month ago is back on the server. Nobody intended it. It carries old commits, it shows up in the branch list, and by Thursday somebody has built a new feature on top of it.

beats.text: No one ran a strange command. One engineer switched to an old local branch and typed git push. The line on screen is all Git said. To understand how an ordinary push resurrects a deleted branch, you need to know one thing a fetch never does by default. Hold on to that zombie branch. Later you make one yourself.
beats.tele: No one ran a strange command. One engineer switched to an old local branch and typed `git push`. The line on screen is all Git said. To understand how an ordinary push resurrects a deleted branch, you need to know one thing a fetch never does by default. Hold on to that zombie branch. Later you make one yourself.

beats.text: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Two subjects today, joined by a common idea: your clone's picture of other repositories is a set of refs that only you maintain. A remote is your name for another repository, and a remote-tracking ref such as origin/main records where one of its branches was at your last fetch.
beats.tele: Welcome back to Git and GitHub Deep Mastery. Pull up a chair. Two subjects today, joined by a common idea: your clone's picture of other repositories is a set of refs that only you maintain. A remote is your name for another repository, and a remote-tracking ref such as `origin/main` records where one of its branches was at your last fetch.

beats.text: First, more than one remote. You build a fork in plain Git, with origin and upstream, and set it up so that you fetch from one repository and push to another. A fork is a second repository on a server, made from the shared one. That setup is called a triangular workflow, and it is where @{upstream} and @{push} finally give different answers. You also meet the small tools around remote URLs: a separate push URL, URL rewriting, renaming and removing a remote.
beats.tele: First, more than one remote. You build a fork in plain Git, with `origin` and `upstream`, and set it up so that you fetch from one repository and push to another. A fork is a second repository on a server, made from the shared one. That setup is called a triangular workflow, and it is where `@{upstream}` and `@{push}` finally give different answers. You also meet the small tools around remote URLs: a separate push URL, URL rewriting, renaming and removing a remote.

beats.text: Second, pruning. A fetch creates and moves remote-tracking refs, but by default it never deletes one. You will see stale refs block a fetch, see what gone means, reproduce the zombie branch from the hook, and then look at the price of pruning automatically.
beats.tele: Second, pruning. A fetch creates and moves remote-tracking refs, but by default it never deletes one. You will see stale refs block a fetch, see what `gone` means, reproduce the zombie branch from the hook, and then look at the price of pruning automatically.

beats.text: Here's what you'll walk away with.
beats.tele: Here's what you'll walk away with.

beats.text: After this video you can:
beats.tele: After this video you can:

beats.text: Configure origin and upstream for a fork and say which one each command uses.
beats.tele: Configure `origin` and `upstream` for a fork and say which one each command uses.

beats.text: Set separate fetch and push URLs, and rename or remove a remote.
beats.tele: Set separate fetch and push URLs, and rename or remove a remote.

beats.text: Explain what pruning deletes and what it never deletes.
beats.tele: Explain what pruning deletes and what it never deletes.

beats.text: Explain how a branch deleted on the server comes back, and prevent it.
beats.tele: Explain how a branch deleted on the server comes back, and prevent it.

beats.text: More than one remote. In one sentence: a repository can have any number of remotes, each with its own URL, refspecs and namespace of remote-tracking refs. Nothing connects them except the objects they share.
beats.tele: More than one remote. In one sentence: a repository can have any number of remotes, each with its own URL, refspecs and namespace of remote-tracking refs. Nothing connects them except the objects they share.

beats.text: So adding a remote named upstream gives you refs/remotes/upstream/* next to refs/remotes/origin/*. Two namespaces. If both name the same commit, it is stored once. On screen is today's clone right after that step: main, origin/main and upstream/main are three names for one commit, 510ee94.
beats.tele: So adding a remote named `upstream` gives you `refs/remotes/upstream/*` next to `refs/remotes/origin/*`. Two namespaces. If both name the same commit, it is stored once. On screen is today's clone right after that step: `main`, `origin/main` and `upstream/main` are three names for one commit, `510ee94`.

beats.text: By convention origin is the repository you push to and upstream is the shared repository you take changes from. That is a convention about names. Git attaches no meaning to either word.
beats.tele: By convention `origin` is the repository you push to and `upstream` is the shared repository you take changes from. That is a convention about names. Git attaches no meaning to either word.

beats.text: A triangular workflow fetches from one repository and pushes to another. Which remote a bare git push uses is decided by settings in a fixed order: branch.<name>.pushRemote, then remote.pushDefault, then branch.<name>.remote, then origin. Which branch name it uses is decided by push.default, from the video before last.
beats.tele: A triangular workflow fetches from one repository and pushes to another. Which remote a bare `git push` uses is decided by settings in a fixed order: `branch.<name>.pushRemote`, then `remote.pushDefault`, then `branch.<name>.remote`, then `origin`. Which branch name it uses is decided by `push.default`, from the video before last.

beats.text: Pruning. In one sentence: a fetch creates and moves remote-tracking refs but by default never deletes one, so branches deleted on the server live on in your clone until you prune.
beats.tele: Pruning. In one sentence: a fetch creates and moves remote-tracking refs but by default never deletes one, so branches deleted on the server live on in your clone until you prune.

beats.text: Three commands. git remote prune --dry-run <remote> previews. git fetch --prune 🟡 CAUTION deletes remote-tracking refs that no longer exist on the server and then fetches. And fetch.prune=true makes every fetch prune.
beats.tele: Three commands. `git remote prune --dry-run <remote>` previews. `git fetch --prune` 🟡 CAUTION deletes remote-tracking refs that no longer exist on the server and then fetches. And `fetch.prune=true` makes every fetch prune.

says: Three commands: git remote prune --dry-run, git fetch --prune, fetch.prune=true

beats.text: Quick quiz. A branch was deleted on the server, and you run git fetch --prune. What does it delete in your clone? A, the remote-tracking ref only. B, the remote-tracking ref and your local branch. Your answer?
beats.tele: Quick quiz. A branch was deleted on the server, and you run `git fetch --prune`. What does it delete in your clone? A, the remote-tracking ref only. B, the remote-tracking ref and your local branch. Your answer?

says: Three commands: git remote prune --dry-run, git fetch --prune, fetch.prune=true
What does git fetch --prune delete in this clone?

beats.text: It's A. What pruning deletes: stale remote-tracking refs and their reflogs. What it never touches: local branches, and their upstream settings. A local branch whose upstream ref has been pruned is reported as gone.
beats.tele: It's A. What pruning deletes: stale remote-tracking refs and their reflogs. What it never touches: local branches, and their upstream settings. A local branch whose upstream ref has been pruned is reported as `gone`.

beats.text: When not to prune automatically? Section 12.16 has the sentence: pruning is forgetting. A remote-tracking ref may be the last name that some commits have in your clone. Prune it and its reflog goes with it. If your clones are the team's only safety net, prune deliberately.
beats.tele: When not to prune automatically? Section 12.16 has the sentence: pruning is forgetting. A remote-tracking ref may be the last name that some commits have in your clone. Prune it and its reflog goes with it. If your clones are the team's only safety net, prune deliberately.

beats.text: A picture helps. Go back to the address book from the first video of this module. Each remote is one entry with its own filing drawer. Two remotes, two drawers. A fetch files fresh copies into a drawer and updates the ones already there. It does not go through the drawer and throw out the bookmarks for things the supplier has discontinued. Pruning is that clean-out.
beats.tele: A picture helps. Go back to the address book from the first video of this module. Each remote is one entry with its own filing drawer. Two remotes, two drawers. A fetch files fresh copies into a drawer and updates the ones already there. It does not go through the drawer and throw out the bookmarks for things the supplier has discontinued. Pruning is that clean-out.

beats.text: Where the picture breaks: in an office, an out-of-date bookmark is clutter. In Git it can be two things at once. It can be a trap, because a local branch that still points at a discontinued name can re-create it with one push. And it can be a rescue, because that stale bookmark may be the only name your clone has for commits that somebody deleted by mistake. The clean-out removes both.
beats.tele: Where the picture breaks: in an office, an out-of-date bookmark is clutter. In Git it can be two things at once. It can be a trap, because a local branch that still points at a discontinued name can re-create it with one push. And it can be a rescue, because that stale bookmark may be the only name your clone has for commits that somebody deleted by mistake. The clean-out removes both.

beats.text: Try it now. Thirty seconds, on paper. Draw three boxes: the shared repository, your clone, and your fork. Add one arrow for fetch and one for push, and write origin or upstream next to the right box. Then say out loud which box your pushes go to.
beats.tele: Try it now. Thirty seconds, on paper. Draw three boxes: the shared repository, your clone, and your fork. Add one arrow for fetch and one for push, and write `origin` or `upstream` next to the right box. Then say out loud which box your pushes go to.

beats.text: Here's the answer. Changes come in from the top and go out at the bottom, to your fork, origin. The pull request, which is a GitHub object and not a Git one, closes the triangle from the bottom box back to the top.
beats.tele: Here's the answer. Changes come in from the top and go out at the bottom, to your fork, `origin`. The pull request, which is a GitHub object and not a Git one, closes the triangle from the bottom box back to the top.

beats.text: Part 1: a fork, in plain Git.
beats.tele: Part 1: a fork, in plain Git.

beats.text: A server-side bare clone stands in for the Fork button. You clone your fork, add upstream, fetch it. git remote -v now has four lines.
beats.tele: A server-side bare clone stands in for the Fork button. You clone your fork, add `upstream`, fetch it. `git remote -v` now has four lines.

beats.text: Two namespaces, origin/* and upstream/*, each with its own HEAD, all naming the same commit.
beats.tele: Two namespaces, `origin/*` and `upstream/*`, each with its own `HEAD`, all naming the same commit.

beats.text: Git has no notion of a fork. The Fork button creates a GitHub object: a server-side copy that stays connected to its parent and shares Git data with it in a repository network. To Git it is one more repository with a URL. According to the documentation, gh repo fork --clone names your fork origin and the parent upstream, the convention used here.
beats.tele: Git has no notion of a fork. The Fork button creates a GitHub object: a server-side copy that stays connected to its parent and shares Git data with it in a repository network. To Git it is one more repository with a URL. According to the documentation, `gh repo fork --clone` names your fork `origin` and the parent `upstream`, the convention used here.

beats.text: Part 2: the triangle.
beats.tele: Part 2: the triangle.

beats.text: Predict: after one commit and a bare git push 🟡, which repository receives the branch? And what do @{upstream} and @{push} resolve to? Say it out loud. I'll wait.
beats.tele: Predict: after one commit and a bare `git push` 🟡, which repository receives the branch? And what do `@{upstream}` and `@{push}` resolve to? Say it out loud. I'll wait.

beats.text: The push went to the fork.
beats.tele: The push went to the fork.

beats.text: @{upstream} is upstream/main, and @{push} is origin/feature/streaming. Two different refs. remote.pushDefault=origin sends every bare push to your fork, whatever the upstream of the branch is, and the branch tracks upstream/main, so git pull takes changes from the shared repository.
beats.tele: `@{upstream}` is `upstream/main`, and `@{push}` is `origin/feature/streaming`. Two different refs. `remote.pushDefault=origin` sends every bare push to your fork, whatever the upstream of the branch is, and the branch tracks `upstream/main`, so `git pull` takes changes from the shared repository.

beats.text: labs/run ch12/push-destination takes the settings one at a time.
beats.tele: `labs/run ch12/push-destination` takes the settings one at a time.

beats.text: With only remote.pushDefault set, the push goes to the fork under the branch's own name, but Git 2.55 cannot answer @{push} under push.default=simple.
beats.tele: With only `remote.pushDefault` set, the push goes to the fork under the branch's own name, but Git 2.55 cannot answer `@{push}` under `push.default=simple`.

beats.text: push.default=current makes the destination a plain function of the branch name. The for-each-ref line is the one to remember in an incident: for every branch, where it pulls from and where it pushes to.
beats.tele: `push.default=current` makes the destination a plain function of the branch name. The `for-each-ref` line is the one to remember in an incident: for every branch, where it pulls from and where it pushes to.

beats.text: branch.<name>.pushRemote overrides the rest for one branch.
beats.tele: `branch.<name>.pushRemote` overrides the rest for one branch.

beats.text: Back in the fork demo. The shared repository has moved.
beats.tele: Back in the fork demo. The shared repository has moved.

beats.text: status.compareBranches, Git 2.54 or later, makes git status report both relationships.
beats.tele: `status.compareBranches`, Git 2.54 or later, makes `git status` report both relationships.

beats.text: Your branch has diverged from upstream/main, which moved to f11a751, and it is up to date with origin/feature/streaming.
beats.tele: Your branch has diverged from `upstream/main`, which moved to `f11a751`, and it is up to date with `origin/feature/streaming`.

beats.text: After a rebase onto the moved upstream, the branch in your fork still holds the old commit, so the push is not a fast-forward.
beats.tele: After a rebase onto the moved upstream, the branch in your fork still holds the old commit, so the push is not a fast-forward.

beats.text: git push --force-with-lease 🔴 DANGEROUS, as every forced push. The five answers are in the previous video. This is the legitimate case: a branch that only you push to, with a lease.
beats.tele: `git push --force-with-lease` 🔴 DANGEROUS, as every forced push. The five answers are in the previous video. This is the legitimate case: a branch that only you push to, with a lease.

beats.text: Bringing the fork's main up to date is a fast-forward from upstream/main and a push to origin.
beats.tele: Bringing the fork's `main` up to date is a fast-forward from `upstream/main` and a push to `origin`.

beats.text: Part 3: URL tools. labs/run ch12/remote-urls.
beats.tele: Part 3: URL tools. `labs/run ch12/remote-urls`.

beats.text: git remote set-url --push 🟡 gives a remote a separate push URL. Here it is deliberately not a repository: a cheap guard that makes pushing to upstream impossible from this clone. The manual warns that a real fetch URL and push URL of one remote must lead to the same repository. For two different places, use two remotes.
beats.tele: `git remote set-url --push` 🟡 gives a remote a separate push URL. Here it is deliberately not a repository: a cheap guard that makes pushing to `upstream` impossible from this clone. The manual warns that a real fetch URL and push URL of one remote must lead to the same repository. For two different places, use two remotes.

beats.text: Several push URLs make one push update several repositories, one after the other and not atomically.
beats.tele: Several push URLs make one push update several repositories, one after the other and not atomically.

beats.text: url.<base>.insteadOf rewrites URLs when they are used. The configuration keeps the URL that was written, and git remote get-url shows what will be contacted.
beats.tele: `url.<base>.insteadOf` rewrites URLs when they are used. The configuration keeps the URL that was written, and `git remote get-url` shows what will be contacted.

beats.text: git remote rename 🟡 moves the remote-tracking refs and rewrites the configuration, including the upstream of main. git remote remove 🟡 deletes the remote-tracking refs with their reflogs and removes upstream settings that pointed at the remote: main is left with none.
beats.tele: `git remote rename` 🟡 moves the remote-tracking refs and rewrites the configuration, including the upstream of `main`. `git remote remove` 🟡 deletes the remote-tracking refs with their reflogs and removes upstream settings that pointed at the remote: `main` is left with none.

beats.text: Part 4: stale refs. labs/run ch12/prune-gone. This runs in Asha's clone. Since she last fetched, feature/reranker was merged and deleted on the server, and the team replaced the branch release by release/1.0.
beats.tele: Part 4: stale refs. `labs/run ch12/prune-gone`. This runs in Asha's clone. Since she last fetched, `feature/reranker` was merged and deleted on the server, and the team replaced the branch `release` by `release/1.0`.

beats.text: git branch -r reads the stale local view: it still lists origin/feature/reranker and origin/release. git ls-remote reads the server.
beats.tele: `git branch -r` reads the stale local view: it still lists `origin/feature/reranker` and `origin/release`. `git ls-remote` reads the server.

beats.text: git remote show origin contacts the server and classifies every branch as tracked, stale or new. Now an ordinary fetch. Predict.
beats.tele: `git remote show origin` contacts the server and classifies every branch as tracked, stale or new. Now an ordinary fetch. Predict.

beats.text: Exit status 1. A stale ref can block a fetch. origin/release still exists, so origin/release/1.0 cannot be created: one ref name cannot be a directory-like prefix of another, in any ref storage format.
beats.tele: Exit status 1. A stale ref can block a fetch. `origin/release` still exists, so `origin/release/1.0` cannot be created: one ref name cannot be a directory-like prefix of another, in any ref storage format.

beats.text: The dry run previews. git fetch --prune deletes the two stale refs and then creates the new one.
beats.tele: The dry run previews. `git fetch --prune` deletes the two stale refs and then creates the new one.

beats.text: Pruning never touches local branches. feature/reranker is still there, and its upstream is now reported as gone. %(upstream:track) gives the same fact to scripts.
beats.tele: Pruning never touches local branches. `feature/reranker` is still there, and its upstream is now reported as `gone`. `%(upstream:track)` gives the same fact to scripts.

beats.text: Part 5: the zombie. Asha switches to that branch. Predict what git pull does and what git push does.
beats.tele: Part 5: the zombie. Asha switches to that branch. Predict what `git pull` does and what `git push` does.

beats.text: git pull fails with a clear message. git push succeeds and re-creates the branch on the server. That is the hook: a branch that the team merged and deleted is back, with old commits. One ordinary push, and nothing looked wrong.
beats.tele: `git pull` fails with a clear message. `git push` succeeds and re-creates the branch on the server. That is the hook: a branch that the team merged and deleted is back, with old commits. One ordinary push, and nothing looked wrong.

beats.text: Delete it on the server again, 🔴 git push origin --delete. Bring main up to date. And delete the local branch with -d, which refuses if the commits are not merged.
beats.tele: Delete it on the server again, 🔴 `git push origin --delete`. Bring `main` up to date. And delete the local branch with `-d`, which refuses if the commits are not merged.

beats.text: With fetch.prune=true every fetch prunes.
beats.tele: With `fetch.prune=true` every fetch prunes.

beats.text: Part 6: the price. labs/run ch12/prune-forgets. Asha has deleted spike/hybrid-search on the server. Your clone has not fetched since.
beats.tele: Part 6: the price. `labs/run ch12/prune-forgets`. Asha has deleted `spike/hybrid-search` on the server. Your clone has not fetched since.

beats.text: Before the prune, your clone still named the two commits, and only the remote-tracking ref contained them. Afterwards the ref is gone, its reflog is gone with it, and git fsck lists the commits as unreachable. They stay in the object database until garbage collection, Git's cleanup of objects that nothing reaches, removes them.
beats.tele: Before the prune, your clone still named the two commits, and only the remote-tracking ref contained them. Afterwards the ref is gone, its reflog is gone with it, and `git fsck` lists the commits as unreachable. They stay in the object database until garbage collection, Git's cleanup of objects that nothing reaches, removes them.

beats.text: Until then git fsck --lost-found can find the tip, 509f067, and a branch gives it a name again. With fetch.prune=true this forgetting happens on every fetch, without a preview.
beats.tele: Until then `git fsck --lost-found` can find the tip, `509f067`, and a branch gives it a name again. With `fetch.prune=true` this forgetting happens on every fetch, without a preview.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: Pushing from an old local branch whose upstream is gone. Root cause: pruning removes the remote-tracking ref but keeps the local branch and its upstream setting, so a push creates the branch on the server again.
beats.tele: Pushing from an old local branch whose upstream is `gone`. Root cause: pruning removes the remote-tracking ref but keeps the local branch and its upstream setting, so a push creates the branch on the server again.

beats.text: Believing git branch -r lists the server's branches. Root cause: it lists remote-tracking refs in your clone, which a default fetch never deletes.
beats.tele: Believing `git branch -r` lists the server's branches. Root cause: it lists remote-tracking refs in your clone, which a default fetch never deletes.

beats.text: Pushing a topic branch to the shared repository in a fork setup. Root cause: without remote.pushDefault or branch.<name>.pushRemote, a branch created from upstream/main has upstream as its remote.
beats.tele: Pushing a topic branch to the shared repository in a fork setup. Root cause: without `remote.pushDefault` or `branch.<name>.pushRemote`, a branch created from `upstream/main` has `upstream` as its remote.

beats.text: Setting fetch.prune=true everywhere and counting on clones as a safety net. Root cause: pruning deletes the ref and its reflog, which may be the last name of commits that were deleted by mistake.
beats.tele: Setting `fetch.prune=true` everywhere and counting on clones as a safety net. Root cause: pruning deletes the ref and its reflog, which may be the last name of commits that were deleted by mistake.

beats.text: Giving one remote a fetch URL and a push URL that are different repositories. Root cause: the manual requires both to lead to the same repository; two places need two remotes.
beats.tele: Giving one remote a fetch URL and a push URL that are different repositories. Root cause: the manual requires both to lead to the same repository; two places need two remotes.

beats.text: Now, out of the lab. You contribute a fix to an open-source evaluation library. Fork, clone, add upstream, branch from upstream/main, push to origin, open the pull request. Inside a company the same triangle appears when a team keeps a patched copy of a vendor repository. The textbook's advice for both: write down which remote is which before the first push.
beats.tele: Now, out of the lab. You contribute a fix to an open-source evaluation library. Fork, clone, add `upstream`, branch from `upstream/main`, push to `origin`, open the pull request. Inside a company the same triangle appears when a team keeps a patched copy of a vendor repository. The textbook's advice for both: write down which remote is which before the first push.

beats.text: On the pruning side, picture a platform team that sets fetch.prune=true in every developer's global configuration to keep branch lists short. It works well for months.
beats.tele: On the pruning side, picture a platform team that sets `fetch.prune=true` in every developer's global configuration to keep branch lists short. It works well for months.

beats.text: Q214: "A branch that was deleted a month ago is back on the server, and nobody intended it. How did it happen, and what do you change?"
beats.tele: Q214: "A branch that was deleted a month ago is back on the server, and nobody intended it. How did it happen, and what do you change?"

beats.text: Answer out loud first. A strong answer reconstructs the sequence from the three kinds of ref: what the deletion removed, what it left behind in some clone, and which ordinary command turned what was left into a new branch on the server. It says how you would find out which clone did it. Then it separates the changes by layer: what each engineer does in their clone, what can be configured in Git, and what a server-side rule could refuse. It also names the cost of the obvious configuration fix.

beats.text: A fetch never deletes a remote-tracking ref unless it prunes. Pruning deletes stale remote-tracking refs and their reflogs and leaves local branches alone, marked gone.
